title: Part 107 Study Guide
subtitle: Seven one-hour lessons, recall cards, worked charts, and practice with explanations.

overview.note: Seven hours is a first preparation cycle. Allow a separate uninterrupted two-hour block for a fresh full exam and additional study when needed.
overview.privacy: Progress is stored in your own browser. This guide contains original instruction and practice, with FAA sources and public sample charts.

lessons.title: Know the limits before you launch
lessons.focus: Operating limits, cloud-clearance math, visual line of sight, and who is responsible.
objectives: Apply the speed, altitude, visibility, and cloud limits to a new scenario.
Explain what the remote PIC and visual observer must do.
Separate a legal limit from a safe decision for the actual conditions.

schedule.label: Recall
schedule.task: Without notes, try the first five cards. Say which altitude reference and unit each number uses.

schedule.label: Learn
schedule.task: Read the sections and work the cloud and structure examples on paper.

schedule.label: Apply
schedule.task: Complete the eight drills without opening the answers first. Mark correct guesses for review.

schedule.label: Fix
schedule.task: Write one corrected rule for each miss. Explain the answer aloud, then retrieve the missed cards again.

sections.title: Start with the numbers and their units
paragraphs: Part 107 covers small unmanned aircraft weighing less than 55 pounds at takeoff, including the battery, payload, guards, and everything attached. Exactly 55 pounds is outside that definition. A certificate does not remove the aircraft's operating limits.

Learn each limit with its reference. The normal altitude limit is 400 feet above the ground beneath the aircraft, not 400 feet above the launch point. Visibility is observed from the control station. Groundspeed measures travel over the ground; a tailwind can increase it even when the aircraft's airspeed is unchanged.

rows: Aircraft weight
Less than 55 lb at takeoff, with everything attached
Groundspeed
No more than 87 knots or 100 mph
Altitude
No higher than 400 ft AGL, with the structure exception below
Flight visibility
At least 3 statute miles from the control station
Cloud separation
At least 500 ft below and 2,000 ft horizontally

sections.title: Cloud clearance can make your ceiling lower
paragraphs: The 400-foot limit and cloud-clearance limits apply together. Being below 400 feet does not make a flight legal if the aircraft is too close to a cloud. Use the same altitude reference before subtracting. A reported cloud base expressed AGL and a proposed height expressed AGL can be compared directly.

For an ordinary flight below an overcast layer, subtract 500 feet from the base, then compare that result with the ordinary 400-foot limit and any lower airspace authorization. The lowest applicable limit controls. Horizontal separation still matters beside individual clouds. Do not invent a rule allowing flight through a gap simply because the aircraft remains visible.

worked.prompt: An overcast base is 750 ft AGL. You have no waiver or structure exception. What is the highest altitude allowed by the normal altitude and below-cloud limits?
steps: Required below-cloud separation is 500 ft.
250 is lower than the normal 400 ft limit.
worked.answer: 250 ft AGL, provided every other applicable requirement is met.
worked.trap: Choosing 400 ft would leave only 350 ft below the clouds.

sections.title: The structure exception has two conditions
paragraphs: You may exceed 400 feet AGL when the aircraft stays within a 400-foot radius of a structure and no higher than 400 feet above its immediate uppermost limit. Both conditions must hold. Once you move outside that radius, the ordinary altitude rule applies again.

This exception does not grant airspace authorization or erase cloud clearance. A LAANC authorization for 150 feet remains a 150-foot authorization beside a tall building. Also check whether the route stays clear of people, other aircraft, and any restricted airspace.

worked.prompt: A tower is 480 ft tall above level ground. The aircraft will remain 250 ft horizontally from it in Class G. Ignoring other limiting conditions only for this calculation, what is the altitude limit under the structure exception?
steps: 250 ft is within the permitted 400 ft radius.
Add 400 ft to the structure's 480 ft height.
worked.answer: 880 ft AGL under the structure exception; this is not permission to disregard the other rules.
worked.trap: The exception concerns distance from a structure, not distance from the pilot.

sections.title: Seeing a video feed is different from seeing the aircraft
paragraphs: The remote PIC, person manipulating the controls, and any visual observer must be able to see the aircraft throughout flight using unaided vision except corrective lenses. At least the PIC and control manipulator, or the observer, must actually exercise that visual observation throughout the flight. You need enough visual information to judge location, attitude, altitude, direction, traffic, and hazards.

An observer can exercise the required observation while a pilot uses a screen, but cannot turn an ordinary Part 107 flight into a relay beyond everyone's required visual capability. Binoculars and a camera feed do not substitute for the required unaided view. If you use an observer, agree on clear communications, traffic calls, and emergency action before launch. One person cannot simultaneously serve as PIC, control manipulator, or observer for more than one drone without an applicable waiver.

sections.title: The PIC makes the decision and stays fit to make it
paragraphs: The remote PIC has final authority and responsibility even when a customer owns the drone or someone else moves the sticks. An uncertificated person may manipulate the controls under direct supervision only when the PIC can immediately take direct control. Before each flight, check the aircraft and the operating environment, brief the crew, confirm working control links, secure the payload, and verify enough power for the intended flight.

Do not fly with a physical or mental condition that interferes with safe operation. Alcohol rules include at least eight hours since drinking, no operating under its influence, and no blood-alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater. Meeting the clock alone does not establish fitness. Yield to other aircraft and stay well clear; never assume a helicopter will see the drone. If an in-flight emergency requires an immediate deviation, deviate only as far as necessary and provide a written explanation if the FAA requests it.

cards.front: What counts toward the less-than-55-lb limit?
cards.back: Everything on board or attached at takeoff, including battery and payload.

cards.front: What is the normal altitude limit?
cards.back: 400 ft AGL, measured above the ground beneath the aircraft; the structure exception has separate conditions.

cards.front: What separation is required below clouds?
cards.back: At least 500 ft below the cloud.

cards.front: What horizontal cloud separation is required?
cards.back: At least 2,000 ft horizontally.

cards.front: What is the maximum groundspeed?
cards.back: 87 knots, equivalent to 100 mph.

cards.front: Where is the 3-statute-mile visibility assessed?
cards.back: From the location of the control station.

cards.front: Who has final authority over the operation?
cards.back: The designated remote pilot in command, even when someone else manipulates the controls.

cards.front: Can a camera feed replace the required unaided view?
cards.back: No. Visual-line-of-sight requirements still apply; corrective lenses are permitted.

cards.front: What are the two structure-exception distances?
cards.back: Within a 400-ft radius of the structure and no higher than 400 ft above its immediate uppermost limit.

cards.front: Does eight hours since drinking always mean fit to fly?
cards.back: No. You also must not be under the influence or have a BAC of 0.04 or greater, and must be fit for safe operation.

drills.prompt: An overcast layer begins at 720 ft AGL. Without a waiver or structure exception, which proposed altitude satisfies both the normal altitude limit and clearance below the layer?
choices: 300 ft AGL
220 ft AGL
400 ft AGL
drills.explanation: 720 − 500 = 220 ft AGL. At 300 ft you would be only 420 ft below the cloud. All other operating requirements must also be satisfied.

drills.prompt: A drone is 300 ft horizontally from a 620-ft tower over level ground in Class G. No other limitation controls. What height is allowed by the structure exception?
choices: 620 ft AGL
700 ft AGL
1,020 ft AGL
drills.explanation: The aircraft is within a 400-ft radius, so the exception permits up to 400 ft above the 620-ft structure: 1,020 ft AGL. It does not remove other applicable requirements.

drills.prompt: A pilot has waited nine hours after drinking but still feels impaired. What is the correct decision?
choices: Do not operate while impaired.
Operate if the flight is below 200 ft.
Operate because the eight-hour period has passed.
drills.explanation: The eight-hour requirement is only one part of the alcohol rule. Operating under the influence remains prohibited, and a condition interfering with safe operation also disqualifies participation.

drills.prompt: A visual observer can see the drone around a building corner, but the remote PIC cannot possibly see it from the control station. No waiver applies. Does the observer's view alone make this an ordinary compliant VLOS operation?
choices: Yes, if communications use a radio.
No; the PIC must still have the required ability to see the aircraft.
Yes, if the drone's camera feed is uninterrupted.
drills.explanation: An observer may exercise visual observation, but the PIC, control manipulator, and any observer must retain the ability required by 107.31(a). An observer does not automatically authorize flight around an obstruction beyond the PIC's visual capability.

drills.prompt: A customer asks a supervised trainee to keep flying after the PIC determines a motor is unsafe. Who has the final operating authority?
choices: The customer who hired the crew.
The person currently holding the controls.
The remote PIC, who must not continue an unsafe flight.
drills.explanation: The PIC has final authority. The system must be safe before flight, and flight cannot continue when the operator knows or has reason to know it is no longer safe.

drills.prompt: A drone beside a building could otherwise use the structure exception, but its airspace authorization limits it to 175 ft AGL. What is the applicable authorized height?
choices: 175 ft AGL
400 ft above the building
400 ft AGL
drills.explanation: The structure exception does not enlarge an airspace authorization. The operation must stay within the authorization's altitude and other conditions.

drills.prompt: A drone is flying level beside a cloud 1,600 ft away horizontally. It remains 250 ft AGL and has 5 miles of visibility. Without a waiver, what is the problem?
choices: Visibility must be at least 5 nautical miles.
The horizontal cloud separation is less than 2,000 ft.
Every cloud requires at least 1,000 ft of vertical separation.
drills.explanation: Normal Part 107 operations require 2,000 ft horizontal cloud separation. Being below 400 ft and having adequate visibility do not replace that requirement.

drills.prompt: An in-flight emergency requires immediate deviation from a Part 107 rule. What does 107.21 permit?
choices: Deviation for the remainder of the job once an emergency begins.
Deviation only after the FAA gives telephone permission.
Deviation only to the extent necessary to meet the emergency.
drills.explanation: Emergency authority is limited to what is necessary. If the FAA requests it, the PIC must provide a written report of the deviation; that is different from the separate safety-event reporting requirement.

lessons.title: Read the chart and identify your airspace
lessons.focus: MSL versus AGL, chart boundaries, airspace authorization, and real chart interpretation.
objectives: Convert between MSL and AGL using the elevation beneath the aircraft.
Identify the airspace at the proposed position and altitude.
Explain when Part 107 airspace authorization is required and what a chart alone cannot establish.

schedule.label: Recall
schedule.task: Retrieve yesterday's missed cards, then state the difference between MSL and AGL before reading.

schedule.label: Learn
schedule.task: Read the airspace table and work both altitude examples. Open the chart and find each feature yourself.

schedule.label: Apply
schedule.task: Complete the eight drills. Point to the evidence on each chart before selecting an answer.

schedule.label: Fix
schedule.task: For every miss, write the feature you overlooked and the correct altitude reference. Retrieve the new cards without rereading.

sections.title: Ask what the altitude is measured from
paragraphs: AGL means above ground level. MSL means above mean sea level. They are two measurements of the same position using different reference surfaces. For a simple problem, altitude MSL equals terrain elevation MSL plus height AGL. To find height AGL, subtract the terrain elevation from altitude MSL.

The ordinary drone limit is AGL. Airport elevations and most charted airspace altitudes are MSL. The airport elevation is not automatically the ground elevation everywhere nearby. If the terrain rises under the flight path while the aircraft holds the same MSL altitude, its height above the ground decreases. Read the reference attached to each number before calculating.

worked.prompt: Terrain directly beneath the drone is 680 ft MSL. The aircraft is at 930 ft MSL. How high is it above that terrain?
steps: Both supplied elevations use MSL, so they can be subtracted.
worked.trap: 930 ft MSL does not mean the drone is 930 ft above the ground.

sourceSections: Chart Users' Guide: Sectional Charts, airport data and airspace information; 14 CFR 107.51(b)

sections.title: Identify the class at the altitude you will occupy
paragraphs: Airspace is three-dimensional. Being inside a shelf's outline on the map does not always put a low-flying drone inside that shelf. Read the floor and ceiling. Class B and C shelf figures are normally hundreds of feet MSL: 40 over 12 means 4,000 over 1,200 ft MSL. SFC means the floor is the surface.

A blue dashed Class D boundary often has a boxed ceiling in hundreds of feet MSL. A minus sign means the stated altitude is excluded. Airspace operating hours can change the answer; check the current Chart Supplement and NOTAMs for part-time areas. Class A generally starts at 18,000 ft MSL, far beyond normal small-drone operations.

sections.title: Learn the Class E distinction carefully
paragraphs: Class E is controlled airspace, but not every Class E operation requires the Part 107 authorization described in 107.41. The airport surface area designated E2 does. An E4 surface extension to a Class D or E surface area does not independently trigger that requirement. Both can use dashed magenta lines, so a line's color alone is insufficient to distinguish the legal designation. Check the airport airspace information and the actual area designation.

A magenta vignette indicates Class E beginning at 700 ft AGL on its shaded side. A blue vignette can indicate a 1,200-ft AGL floor. Unless another designation changes the location, the low airspace underneath is Class G. Do not confuse the soft shaded edge with a dashed magenta surface boundary. A chart is a starting point, not proof that a specific flight is permitted today.
sourceSections: Chart Users' Guide: Class E airspace; AIM 3-2-6; FAA Order 7210.3, 19-6-1; 14 CFR 107.41

sections.title: Find the evidence on an actual chart
paragraphs: Open Figure 22 and find Sandpoint near the top. Its airport information includes 2131, the field elevation in feet MSL. The AWOS weather frequency and CTAF are different items with different jobs. A CTAF helps pilots coordinate airport traffic; listening or making a radio call does not provide a drone airspace authorization.

Obstacle labels also carry two references. Near Priest River, the obstruction labeled 2630 with (215) below it has a top elevation of 2,630 ft MSL and a height of 215 ft AGL. Subtracting the two gives the ground elevation at its base. Large two-part maximum-elevation figures describe a chart quadrangle, not permission for a drone to climb to that altitude. Use the legend instead of guessing from a number's size.
sections.figureNote: Historical FAA training chart; use it to practice reading symbols, not to plan a current flight.

worked.prompt: A training scenario places the drone 180 ft above Sandpoint's published field elevation. What MSL altitude corresponds to that position?
steps: Read 2,131 ft MSL from the airport data.
Add the stated 180-ft height above the field: 2,131 + 180.
worked.answer: 2,311 ft MSL. This calculation assumes the scenario's stated field reference; it does not establish surrounding terrain elevations.
worked.trap: The adjacent weather frequency is not an elevation, and an airport's elevation is not a blanket terrain value.

sourceSections: FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 22; Chart Users' Guide: Airport Data and Obstructions; 14 CFR 107.41

sections.title: FAA September 2026 example: Millville
paragraphs: The FAA’s September 2026 advisory asks readers to identify the airspace at Millville Municipal and decide whether a drone flight needs ATC authorization. Start with the airport symbol and the boundary around it; the answer comes from the chart, not from remembering an airport name.
sections.figureNote: This is the FAA’s actual public sample image. Try the question before opening the worked answer.

worked.prompt: At Millville Municipal (MIV), which surface airspace applies, and must a Part 107 operation obtain ATC authorization?
steps: Find the magenta airport symbol labeled MILLVILLE MUNI (MIV).
Read the dashed magenta airport-surface boundary. The FAA identifies this sample as airport surface Class E.
Apply the airport-surface Class E authorization requirement rather than treating every area of Class E alike.
worked.answer: The FAA’s keyed answer is airport surface Class E, with ATC authorization required.
worked.trap: A magenta airport symbol means an airport without an operating tower; it does not establish that the surrounding surface airspace is Class G.

sections.title: Authorization is a separate step
paragraphs: Request required airspace authorization through LAANC or FAA DroneZone. A UAS Facility Map grid value shows an altitude that may be authorized without further coordination; the grid itself is not approval. Read the approval's location, altitude, dates, and conditions. Do not substitute a tower radio call for the authorization process.

Also check current flight restrictions, NOTAMs, prohibited or restricted areas, and airport activity. A Class G location can still be inside a restriction, and you may not interfere with airport operations. Finish each chart task by stating three things: my position, my altitude and reference, and the applicable rule or approval.

cards.front: How do you convert MSL altitude to AGL height?
cards.back: Subtract terrain elevation MSL directly beneath the aircraft from the aircraft's altitude MSL.

cards.front: What does 40 over 12 on a Class C shelf mean?
cards.back: A ceiling of 4,000 ft MSL and floor of 1,200 ft MSL.

cards.front: What does SFC mean on an airspace floor label?
cards.back: The airspace begins at the surface.

cards.front: Which B, C, and D drone operations require authorization?
cards.back: Operations inside Class B, C, or D require prior ATC authorization under 107.41.

cards.front: What does a dashed blue boundary usually identify?
cards.back: Class D airspace. Check its ceiling and effective times.

cards.front: What does a magenta vignette mean?
cards.back: Class E starts at 700 ft AGL on the shaded side, unless another airspace designation changes the location.

cards.front: Which Class E surface designation requires 107.41 authorization?
cards.back: E2: the surface area designated for an airport. E4 extensions do not independently trigger that requirement.

cards.front: What is the parenthesized number under an obstacle elevation?
cards.back: The obstacle's height above ground level; the top number is its elevation MSL.

cards.front: Does a UAS Facility Map grid value authorize a flight?
cards.back: No. It supports authorization processing; obtain and follow the actual required approval.

cards.front: Does Class G mean no flight restrictions apply?
cards.back: No. Check TFRs, prohibited/restricted areas, airport activity, and all other applicable rules.

drills.prompt: A drone holds 1,060 ft MSL above terrain at 790 ft MSL. What is its height above that terrain?
choices: 270 ft AGL
790 ft AGL
1,850 ft AGL
drills.explanation: AGL height is 1,060 − 790 = 270 ft. Both supplied values are MSL elevations, so subtract them.

drills.prompt: In Figure 20, the Class C shelf north of Norfolk International is labeled 40 over 12. Ignoring other designations, does that shelf itself contain a drone at 350 ft MSL?
choices: Yes; it begins 120 ft above the ground.
Yes; every location inside the outline is Class C down to the surface.
No; this shelf begins at 1,200 ft MSL.
drills.explanation: The floor is 1,200 ft MSL. The 40/12 shelf alone does not include a position at 350 ft MSL. The complete location still needs to be checked for other airspace and restrictions.

drills.prompt: At a site where the only controlled airspace begins at 700 ft AGL, a drone will remain at 300 ft AGL. Which class does it occupy?
choices: Class E, because the map is shaded magenta.
Class G below the Class E floor.
Class D below the Class E floor.
drills.explanation: With no other designation, the space below the 700-ft Class E floor is Class G. The transition area's map outline does not make Class E extend to the ground.

drills.prompt: In Figure 22, the obstruction near Priest River is labeled 2630 with (215) beneath it. What ground elevation at the obstruction's base follows from those labels?
choices: 2,415 ft MSL
215 ft MSL
2,845 ft MSL
drills.explanation: The top is 2,630 ft MSL and the structure is 215 ft AGL. The base is therefore 2,630 − 215 = 2,415 ft MSL.

drills.prompt: A current FAA designation identifies your site as an E4 surface extension, outside any E2, B, C, or D area. Does the E4 designation by itself require a 107.41 authorization?
choices: Yes; every Class E area requires one.
Yes, unless the airport has a control tower.
No; the Class E authorization requirement applies to E2 airport surface areas.
drills.explanation: FAA airspace-authorization guidance distinguishes E2 from other Class E. An E4 extension does not independently trigger 107.41, though other rules and restrictions remain applicable.

drills.prompt: A required airspace authorization has not been issued. A UAS Facility Map shows 200 in the grid covering the site. What does that value allow you to conclude?
choices: Any Part 107 drone may fly to 200 ft without applying.
Up to 200 ft may be eligible for approval without further ATC coordination; it is not an authorization.
The area is Class G below 200 ft.
drills.explanation: Facility Map values support the approval process. They do not establish the airspace class or replace the required authorization.

drills.prompt: Using Figure 22's Sandpoint airport elevation, a training scenario places a drone 240 ft above the field. What is the resulting altitude MSL?
choices: 2,371 ft MSL
2,131 ft MSL
1,891 ft MSL
drills.explanation: Sandpoint's published field elevation is 2,131 ft MSL. Add the scenario's 240-ft height: 2,371 ft MSL. This is a calculation from the stated field reference, not a determination of surrounding terrain.

drills.prompt: A part-time Class D tower closes before your planned flight. What should you use to determine the airspace that applies after closing?
choices: Assume all airspace becomes Class G when any tower closes.
Treat the entire former Class D as permanently Class D.
Check the current Chart Supplement, chart notes, and applicable NOTAMs for the published status.
drills.explanation: A part-time Class D area may become Class E or Class G during other times. The published status determines which rules apply; tower closure alone is not a universal answer.

lessons.title: Use the current rules for the flight you are planning
lessons.focus: Registration, Remote ID, night flight, operations over people and vehicles, recency, and reporting.
objectives: Distinguish registration, Remote ID, recency, airspace authorization, and a waiver.
Identify the main conditions for night flight and the four operations-over-people categories.
Apply the calendar-month recency rule and safety-event reporting thresholds.

schedule.task: Read the current-rule sections and compare the four people categories. Work the calendar-month example.

schedule.task: Complete the eight drills. For each one, name the rule that controls the answer.
